case_title: R. Shaji v. State of Kerala
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (as stated in prosecution case: 'He was also related to the appellant'); the victim was also trusted with free access to the appellant's house
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.120-B; IPC s.201 r/w s.120-B; IPC s.364 r/w s.120-B
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence; recovery evidence (chopper, skull, van, glove, rope); DNA and forensic evidence; medical (post-mortem) opinion; eyewitness and last-seen testimony
confession: Disclosure statement by the appellant leading to recovery of chopper and skull; relied on for the recoveries. No confession to the killing itself is stated.
aggravating_circumstances: Dismemberment of the body; prior threat to chop the victim into pieces; conspiracy with another accused
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.120-B (life imprisonment and fine of Rs. one lakh); s.201 r/w s.120-B (3 years, fine Rs. 2,000); s.364 r/w s.120-B (7 years RI, fine Rs. 5,000); sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Criminal Appeal No. 86 of 2006 dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 r/w s.120-B; s.201 r/w s.120-B; s.364 r/w s.120-B
neutral_facts: The victim, who had worked as a driver for a vehicle used by the accused's wife, developed an intimate relationship with the accused's wife. Relatives intervened and the victim was told to leave the city. The accused reportedly said that if he got hold of the victim he would chop him into pieces. On 15 February 2005 the victim was seen at a bar and a roadside eatery with a second accused. Witnesses saw the victim transferred from a motorcycle into a Maruti van, which the first accused was seen driving, and which left the city towards a forest area around midnight. An auto-rickshaw driver saw a man standing beside the van. The victim was not seen alive again. Between 16 and 19 February 2005, body parts, including legs, a torso, hands and a head in a plastic cover, were found in a backwater lake. The victim's father identified the torso and hands, and DNA analysis matched the remains with the parents' DNA. Post-mortem injuries were consistent with dismemberment using a chopper. A chopper was recovered from the lake on the accused's disclosure; it had blood stains and hair on it. A skull was recovered after digging at a location shown by the accused. A glove and a plastic rope were also recovered at his instance. Police collected blood and hair samples from the van floor, and the hair matched the victim's. Witnesses at the bar and eatery identified the accused and the second accused. The chopper maker and a forensic surgeon gave evidence on the chopper.
physical_harm: Death of victim; body dismembered into parts (legs, torso, hands, head, skull) recovered from the lake
number_of_offences: 3 charged (s.302 r/w s.120-B; s.201 r/w s.120-B; s.364 r/w s.120-B); 3 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Yes: court found a conspiracy to eliminate the victim. The chopper was ordered and handed to the appellant in early January 2005, before the killing.
motive: Accepted by the court: the appellant's animosity arising from the victim's intimacy with the appellant's wife
key_evidence_accepted: DNA report identifying remains; recovery of chopper on disclosure (PW-77); chopper maker's evidence; forensic surgeon's opinion that dismemberment was possible with the chopper; hair of victim found in van; call details between appellant and van owner; identification by PW-8, PW-9, PW-11, PW-12 and PW-13; last-seen evidence; testimony of PW-12 accepted
witness_credibility: PW-12 (prime witness) not disbelieved in toto, though his photograph-based identification was unconvincing; PW-8 and PW-13 knew the appellant; PW-10 and PW-12 presence accepted; the court applied quality over quantity
post_offence_conduct: Court noted the appellant's disclosures leading to recoveries; PW-11 evidence that the appellant posted a letter in the victim's name purporting he was going to Bombay, which the court found insignificant; the van was returned and later recovered
trial_duration: offence: 15/16.2.2005; trial judgment: 3.1.2006; High Court: 10.12.2009; Supreme Court: 4.2.2013
legal_representation: Appellant: Dr. S. Gopakumaran Nair, T.G. Narayanan Nair, K.N. Madhusoodhanan. State: R. Basanth, Ramesh Babu M.R., Karthik Ashok, P.V. Dinesh
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge sheet filed against five persons; trial conducted against two (appellant and A-2); A-3 and A-4 separately tried and convicted; A-5 absconding
procedural_irregularity: Alleged: no test identification parade held; s.164 statements not put on record or marked. Court found the non-marking issue was raised first in the High Court and did not vitiate the trial; TIP held to lose significance.
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions Court, Kottayam): convicted, life imprisonment and other sentences. High Court: appeal dismissed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Circumstances proved point only to appellant's guilt; DNA established the remains; prosecution witnesses had no reason to depose falsely; TIP would have been a formality as witnesses knew the appellant
defence_argument: No motive; circumstantial case with incomplete chain; no test identification parade; s.164 statements not exhibited; no blood group on chopper so recovery unreliable; PW-12 could not identify; identification of body by mole unreliable
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain beyond reasonable doubt; conspiracy proof by circumstantial evidence; recovery on disclosure makes blood group matching immaterial; motive relevant in circumstantial cases; quality over quantity of witnesses; s.164 statements usable for corroboration and contradiction; accomplice evidence admissible with caution; TIP significance depends on facts
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra AIR 1984 SC 1622; Babu v. State of Kerala (2010) 9 SCC 189; Vijay@Chinee v. State of M.P. (2010) 8 SCC 191; Prabhu Babaji Navie v. State of Bombay AIR 1956 SC 51; John Pandian v. State (2010) 14 SCC 129; Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras AIR 1957 SC 614; Mir Nagvi Askari v. CBI AIR 2010 SC 528; Laxmipat Choraria v. State of Maharashtra AIR 1968 SC 938
